title: String inverters versus microinverters for a home solar PV system
subtitle: Choosing the inverter architecture that matches your roof and budget
excerpt: A string inverter converts the DC output of all panels in a series string together. A microinverter sits behind each panel and converts it individually. The choice affects performance under partial shading, installation cost, monitoring granularity, and long-term maintenance. For a simple unshaded south-facing roof, string is cheaper and fine. For any shaded, split-pitch, or multi-orientation roof, microinverters or power optimisers prevent the partial-shade penalty from collapsing the whole array's output.
sourceNotes: Solar Trade Association (STA) Best Practice Guide for domestic PV 2024. Enphase IQ8 and SolarEdge HD-Wave inverter technical documentation. BEIS Feed-In Tariff and SEG guidance 2024.

glossaryTerms.definition: A single central inverter connected to all panels in the array wired in series (a string). The inverter converts the combined DC output to AC. The string operates at the lowest-performing panel's level — one shaded panel reduces the output of the whole string.
A small inverter fixed behind each solar panel that converts that panel's DC output to AC independently. Shading one panel does not affect the rest.

Maximum Power Point Tracking. The algorithm that adjusts the inverter's input voltage to extract the maximum power from the panels at any given irradiance level. A string inverter has one MPPT for the whole string; microinverters have one per panel.

A panel-level DC-DC converter that sits behind each panel, tracking its individual MPPT, then passing the optimised DC to a central string inverter. A compromise between string and micro architectures.

content.text: In a
string inverter

system, all panels are wired in series. Their voltages add together; their current is limited by the weakest panel. If one panel produces 90% of its rated output due to shading, the current of the entire string drops. On a roof with a chimney stack, a dormer, or overhanging tree branches, this penalty can be substantial, a 20% shading on two panels in a 12-panel string can reduce total output by 40% or more during shadow-passing hours.
When string inverters are sufficient
All panels face the same direction (south, south-east, or south-west) within 30° of each other.
The roof face is unshaded by adjacent chimneys, dormers, trees, or neighbouring buildings between 9 am and 3 pm throughout the year.
Budget is the main constraint. String inverters cost much less than
microinverter
s. For a 12-panel array, microinverters add a significant premium to the total cost.
When microinverters or
power optimiser
s are worth the premium
Panels split across two roof faces at different orientations, common on L-shaped houses. Each face can be on its own microinverter string and track its own peak.

Any intermittent shading from a chimney, satellite dish, or tree. Even a shadow path crossing one panel for two hours per day on a 12-panel south-facing array can reduce annual yield by 400 to 600 kWh without panel-level
MPPT

Panel-level monitoring is required, for example, where the owner wants to detect a failing panel quickly. String inverters report total string output; the failure of one panel shows up only as a small overall dip.
The power optimiser middle ground

A power optimiser gives panel-level MPPT while using a single central inverter for AC conversion. The SolarEdge system is the main UK example. The cost premium is about half that of microinverters. The central inverter is still a single point of failure. With microinverters, a failed unit affects only one panel.
Worked comparison: a Victorian semi in Bristol

South-facing roof, 12 panels (4.2 kWp), chimney stack shading 2 panels for 3 hours per day on clear days (roughly 100 days per year). String inverter annual yield estimate: 3,400 kWh. With microinverters: 3,800 kWh. Difference: 400 kWh per year. The extra yield pays back the microinverter premium in approximately 11 years. The chimney can be treated as a permanent feature; the microinverter investment pays for itself before the expected 20-year inverter life is reached.
